audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet Amaziah, Edom war, Israel-Judah conflict, assassination, Azariah, and Jeroboam II narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for execution of regicides without descendant punishment, Edomite mass killing, royal challenge and parable, defeat and wall breach, temple plunder and hostages, assassination, adolescent coronation, imperial restoration, Jonah reference, affliction, and deliverance through a negatively evaluated king.

verses.restored: In second year of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah became king.
Twenty-five years old was he when he became king, and twenty-nine years he reigned in Jerusalem. Name of his mother was Jehoaddan from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in eyes of YHWH, yet not like David his father; according to all Joash his father did, he did.
Only high places were not removed; people were still sacrificing and burning incense at high places.
When kingdom was strengthened in his hand, he struck his servants who had struck king his father.

But sons of those who struck him he did not put to death, according to what is written in scroll of Torah of Moses, which YHWH commanded, saying, Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, and sons shall not be put to death for fathers; each shall be put to death for his own sin.
He struck ten thousand of Edom in Valley of Salt and captured Sela in battle; he called its name Joktheel to this day.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu king of Israel, saying, Come, let us see one another face to face.

Jehoash king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thornbush in Lebanon sent to cedar in Lebanon, saying, Give your daughter to my son as wife. But a wild animal in Lebanon passed and trampled thornbush.
Striking, you have struck Edom, and your heart has lifted you. Be honored and stay in your house. Why stir yourself into harm, so you fall, you and Judah with you?
But Amaziah did not listen. Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah saw one another face to face at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.
Judah was struck before Israel, and each fled to his tent.

Jehoash king of Israel seized Amaziah king of Judah, son of Jehoash son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh. He came to Jerusalem and broke wall of Jerusalem from Ephraim Gate to Corner Gate, four hundred cubits.
He took all gold and silver, all vessels found in house of YHWH and treasuries of king's house, and hostages, and returned to Samaria.
Remaining acts of Jehoash, what he did, his might, and how he fought Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Israel?
Jehoash lay with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with kings of Israel. Jeroboam his son became king in his place.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
Remaining acts of Amaziah, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Judah?
They conspired against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.
They carried him on horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in city of David.
All people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He built Elath and restored it to Judah after king lay with his fathers.
In fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel became king in Samaria and reigned forty-one years.
He did evil in eyes of YHWH; he did not turn from all sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.
He restored border of Israel from entrance of Hamath to sea of Arabah, according to word of YHWH, Divine of Israel, spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, prophet from Gath-hepher.
For YHWH saw affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter; there was none restrained, none released, and no helper for Israel.
YHWH had not spoken to blot out name of Israel from under heavens, so he saved them by hand of Jeroboam son of Joash.
Remaining acts of Jeroboam, all he did, his might, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah/Israel, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Israel?
Jeroboam lay with his fathers, with kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son became king in his place.

translation_notes: Verse 6 explicitly rejects inherited criminal punishment. It is a major safeguard against executing children for parents, collective family guilt, blood-feud logic, and political purges.
Amaziah's execution of his father's killers is still capital punishment under royal power; the restraint toward their children does not automatically validate the executions themselves.
The killing of ten thousand Edomites and seizure/renaming of Sela are conquest violence. Edomites are not a timeless enemy, and modern territorial claims cannot be built from this account.
The thornbush-and-cedar parable challenges royal pride but uses a marriage proposal as political imagery. Daughters are not diplomatic property.
Amaziah rejects warning and brings defeat, wall destruction, plunder, and hostages upon others. A leader's pride imposes costs on people who did not choose the challenge.
Hostages are human beings under coercion, not inventory beside temple treasure.
Amaziah's assassination lacks narrated due process. His earlier legal restraint does not protect him from the same political violence that killed his father.
Azariah is made king at sixteen; adolescence must not be romanticized as readiness for unaccountable rule.
Jeroboam II receives a negative moral evaluation yet becomes an instrument of relief because the people's suffering is seen. Help is not proof that a ruler or regime is righteous.
Border restoration and references to Damascus/Hamath require historical, textual, and geopolitical audit and cannot ground modern expansionism.
safety_note: Center the chapter's rejection of inherited punishment while refusing to glorify executions, Edomite mass killing, conquest, hostages, adolescent kingship, assassination, or territorial expansion. A ruler's pride can expose an entire population to consequences, and relief for suffering people does not sanctify the ruler through whom it comes.
